About this video

Transcript

Imagine it's 1970, and you hide a $100 bill under your mattress. You forget about it for 56 years, and find it again today. It's still $100. But now it only buys about as much as $12 did back then. So where did the other $88 go? The answer is inflation: the slow, steady rise of prices across the whole economy. To measure it, the government tracks a huge basket of things people buy: food, rent, fuel, clothes, transport, and doctor visits. Every month, it records the prices of about 80,000 items, in thousands of stores, rental homes, and doctors' offices. Put it all together, and you get one number: the Consumer Price Index. Let's make that real. Here's what some everyday things cost in 1980, according to government price surveys, and what they cost now. A pound of white bread went from 51 cents to $1.83. A dozen eggs, from 84 cents to $2.27. A pound of coffee, from $3.14 to $9.33. And a gallon of gas, from $1.25 to $4.48. Different things rise at different speeds. But the direction is almost always the same: up. Here's the full index for the United States since 1950. Notice something? It almost never goes down. Something that cost $1 in 1970 costs about $8.66 today. That's prices rising by almost 4% a year, on average, for more than half a century. So why do prices keep climbing? The simplest answer: when more money chases the same amount of stuff, prices go up. Economists call one version demand-pull inflation. People, businesses, and governments try to spend more than the economy can produce, often when borrowing is cheap, so sellers raise prices. The other is cost-push inflation. When oil spikes or factories shut down, it costs more to make things, and those costs get passed on to you. Most of the time, inflation is slow and quiet. But sometimes, it explodes. In March 1980, prices were rising almost 15% a year. And in June 2022, after the pandemic, inflation hit about 9%, the highest in four decades. When inflation gets out of hand, central banks fight back with one main weapon: interest rates. Higher rates make borrowing more expensive. People and businesses borrow less and spend less, demand cools down, and prices calm down with it. In 1981, to crush double-digit inflation, the Federal Reserve pushed its key interest rate to about 19%. It worked, but it also helped trigger a painful recession. In 2022, it raised rates from almost zero to over 5% in about a year and a half, the fastest climb in four decades. So shouldn't the goal be zero inflation? Surprisingly, no. The US Federal Reserve aims for about 2%. Because falling prices can be even worse. If you expect things to be cheaper next month, you wait. Businesses sell less, cut jobs, and prices fall even further. A little inflation keeps money moving. But inflation doesn't treat everyone the same. If you keep your savings in cash, you lose. Your money quietly buys less every single year. If you owe money at a fixed interest rate, you can actually win, because you pay it back with dollars that are worth less. And if your pay rises slower than prices, you're getting a pay cut, even if your salary never changes. And that last one matters more than you might think. In 1970, a typical non-manager worker in America earned about $3.40 an hour. Today, it's about $32.60. That looks like a massive raise. But adjust for inflation, and the picture changes. In today's dollars, that worker's hourly pay is only about 4% higher than it was in 1973. Most of the raise was eaten by rising prices. This doesn't count benefits like health insurance, but the lesson stands: what matters isn't how much you earn. It's what your pay can buy. Here's a handy trick. Divide 70 by the inflation rate, and you get roughly how many years it takes for prices to double. At 2%, prices double in about 35 years. At 7%, in just 10. That's why many people don't leave long-term savings sitting in cash. They look for places where money can grow at least as fast as prices, knowing that every option comes with its own risks. This channel isn't financial advice. But the lesson is simple: money that sits still slowly melts. So, where did your $100 go? Nowhere. It just shrank, a few cents at a time.
